Rubin DP2: a basic catalog and image tutorial notebook¶

Audience: astronomers who know a little Python but are new to Rubin data.
Platform: Rubin Science Platform (RSP), data.lsst.cloud.
Suggested session: 45–60 minutes; optional cells can be skipped.
References: The four core official tutorials are

102.2: Catalog queries with TAP,

201.01: Object table,

104.5: Image subsets with the Butler,

205.1: PSF for deep coadd images.

Check the dp2 website for more details: DP2 tutorials.

By the end of this tutorial, you will query a small Object sample, understand its photometry and flags, retrieve a coadd cutout image, and compare a point-source PSF model with real pixels.

Route through the notebook¶

  1. Before the exercises: survey, release, glossary, photometry, flags, and RSP setup.
  2. Part 1 — Object catalogs: find columns, run a cone search, make a simple selection, and save the results.
  3. Part 2 — Images and models: identify a coadd, retrieve a cutout image, inspect its mask and PSF, and make a simple model/residual image.
  4. Final optional appendix: a few DP1/NERSC examples for differences between data releases and platforms.

This is a short synthesis, not a replacement for their full examples.

Before the exercises: what are Rubin and DP2?¶

The NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile conducts the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST): repeated optical imaging that lets us study both faint structure and changes over time. The six bands, u, g, r, i, z, y, progress approximately from bluer to redder light. Repeated observations can be combined for depth or kept separate for time-domain studies.

DP2 is Data Preview 2, a commissioning/science-validation dataset, rather than a full ten-year survey or a numbered annual LSST Data Release. It contains LSSTCam observations from April 2025–January 2026, processed with Rubin Science Pipelines v30. DP1 used the smaller LSST Commissioning Camera (ComCam) and v29 processing; DP0.2 is simulated data. IDs and measured values should not be assumed to match across releases.

The documentation currently distinguishes Early DP2, released 27 July 2026, from full DP2, expected in October–December 2026. Early DP2 has catalogs, including visit/difference measurements, but its released science-image pixels are deep coadds. This notebook needs only those coadds. For this tutorial, Early DP2 is sufficient for Object queries, coadd cutouts, and coadd PSF analysis. You can also construct catalog-based light curves already; full DP2 enables inspecting the corresponding individual-epoch and difference-image pixels. Check the DP2 landing page for the current release state.

Coverage and depth: look before choosing a target¶

DP2 coadds cover about 3,000 square degrees, whereas single-epoch catalogs cover about 15,000 square degrees. A catalog detection outside the coadd footprint need not have a coadd available. Depth and available bands vary with position; commissioning cadence and image quality are not predictions for the final LSST survey.

Depth describes how faint a source can be measured. A larger limiting AB magnitude means fainter light. A PSF limiting magnitude describes point-source sensitivity; it is not a universal galaxy completeness limit. At the Extended Chandra Deep Field South (ECDFS) field center, the documentation reports an i-band coadd 5-sigma PSF limit of about 25.87 mag; this is a local value, not the depth of every pixel in ECDFS. Source: DP2 observations, coverage and depth.

Official DP2 coverage map: blue shows visit density; outlined tracts mark planned coadd regions. Figure reproduced from the DP2 observations page, Rubin Observatory / AURA (2026). Not every outlined region has pixels in every band.

Official DP2 i-band coadd PSF limiting-magnitude map. Read the color scale as point-source depth, not object density. Figure reproduced from the DP2 observations page, Rubin Observatory / AURA (2026).

Glossary: observations, catalogs, and images¶

Term Meaning in this notebook
Exposure / visit An exposure is one camera integration/readout. A visit is the observing unit; in DP2 a visit consists of one exposure.
Detector One camera sensor. A processed visit image is normally identified by visit and detector, together with its other dataset dimensions.
Band / physical filter i is a band; a physical filter identifies the actual instrument filter.
Object A sky object measured in the coadds, with per-band measurements. dp2.Object contains retained deblended objects, not parent blend rows.
Source / ForcedSource A Source is detected in a visit image. ForcedSource measures at known Object positions in individual visits, even when an epoch has weak signal.
DiaSource / DiaObject A difference-image detection / an associated object from difference-image analysis. These IDs are not interchangeable with Object IDs.
Coadd (deep_coadd) Images from multiple visits combined on a shared sky grid. DP2 uses cell-based coadds represented by lsst.images.CellCoadd.
Template / difference image A reference image / the result of subtracting that reference from a visit. Useful for variability; not used here.
Footprint / deblending A footprint is a detected region of pixels. / The set of image pixels belonging to a detected region of light. Deblending separates overlapping light into child objects.
PSF Point spread function: the local image of a point source after atmosphere, optics, detector, and processing effects. It varies across the image.
WCS / sky projection The mapping between sky coordinates and pixel coordinates. TAP coord_ra, coord_dec are ICRS (International Celestial Reference System) degrees.
Mask / variance Per-pixel condition indicators / an image uncertainty estimate in squared image units.

See source detection and measurement and DP2 data products for terminology and product availability.

Glossary: finding and identifying data¶

Term Practical meaning
objectId Integer key for an Object row. Preserve as a 64-bit integer or exact string, never a float.
parentObjectId Links deblend siblings to their parent blend. 0 means the object has no parent blend.
Skymap / tract / patch / cell An all-sky tiling / a large tile / a smaller overlapping tile / a small coadd processing region. Tract and patch are spatial indices, not object IDs.
Dataset type The Butler product name, such as deep_coadd, object, or object_scarlet_models. TAP and Butler names differ.
dataId Dimension values identifying a Butler product: for a coadd, typically skymap, tract, patch, and band. It is not the catalog objectId.
DatasetRef A Butler reference to a particular dataset, carrying its dataId and provenance. Use a reference when overlaps return several candidates.
Repository / collection Butler configuration / the selected group or processing lineage of datasets. RSP uses dp2 for both in these examples.
TAP / ADQL Table Access Protocol / its astronomy-aware query language, similar to SQL. Best for small catalog selections.
Butler Rubin's Python interface for locating and reading datasets and components. Best here for pixels, WCS, PSF, and models.
RSP Portal / Notebooks / APIs Graphical searching / hosted Python analysis / programmatic service access.

Two access routes meet at the sky position: TAP → Object row → coordinates → Butler → image. The image's absolute tract pixels and the cutout's local array indices could be different. Always convert using the WCS or take the cutout origin into account. NumPy arrays use [y, x].

A photometry column guide¶

Here {b} stands for a band, for example i_psfFlux or g_cModelMag. Read the live schema in Part 1 to confirm units and definitions.

Column family What it measures; a useful first application
{b}_psfFlux, psfFluxErr, psfMag, psfMagErr A forced PSF fit and its uncertainty; a useful choice for point sources. Fluxes are in nJy; magnitudes are AB.
{b}_cModelFlux, cModelMag and errors A PSF-convolved exponential + de Vaucouleurs model; an estimate of total galaxy light. Check {b}_cModel_flag.
{b}_kronFlux, kronFluxErr, kronRad Adaptive aperture photometry; radius is in pixels, not arcsec. Check {b}_kronFlux_flag.
{b}_ap03Flux, ap06Flux, … Circular-aperture measurements; the suffix gives the aperture radius in pixels. Apertures can omit outer light and include neighbors.
{b}_gaap1p0Flux, … Gaussian aperture and PSF photometry; useful for consistent colors, not generally total flux.
{b}_sersicFlux, sersic_index, sersic_reff_major/minor Multiband parametric galaxy model; major/minor effective radii are in arcsec. This model differs from the non-parametric Scarlet deblend model.
refBand, refExtendedness, {b}_extendedness Reference band and morphology classifiers; point-like/extended is not a confirmed star/galaxy label.
{b}_blendedness, detect_fromBlend Light contamination indicator / membership in a deblended system. Interpret with the documented definition.

For positive calibrated flux, $m_{AB}=31.4-2.5\log_{10}(f_{nJy})$ and $\sigma_m\simeq(2.5/\ln 10)\sigma_f/f$ at high signal-to-noise. Non-positive flux has no ordinary logarithmic magnitude; retain the flux and uncertainty instead. Forced measurements in a band do not imply an independent detection in that band. Sources: galaxy photometry and TAP magnitude conversion.

Quality flags: know which measurement you are using¶

Column or family How to read it
{b}_psfFlux_flag, {b}_cModel_flag, {b}_kronFlux_flag True/1 indicates failure of that measurement. Use the flag matching the flux you analyze.
{b}_inputCount Number of inputs at the position; >0 checks coverage. It is not a failure flag.
{b}_invalidPsfFlag A problem with the PSF model.
{b}_pixelFlags_saturatedCenter, interpolatedCenter Saturation or interpolation near the centroid; often relevant to photometry.
{b}_pixelFlags_* Conditions summarized over a footprint or its center. Some legacy bad/edge/suspect flags are deprecated for Object; avoid copying Source cuts blindly.
shape_flag, sersic_no_data_flag, sersic_unknown_flag Problems with shape measurement or the Sérsic fit. Check numeric values as well.
{b}_calib_psf_used, {b}_calib_psf_reserved Calibration-selection indicators, not failure flags.
detect_fromBlend, detect_isIsolated Context about detection/deblending, not universal quality exclusions.

Apply cuts in every band needed for a color. Missing/NULL flags do not establish a good measurement. No single set of flags guarantees a pure, complete sample; inspect what your cuts remove. The worked selection follows the principles in official flag-use guidance.

For more details in all available columns and comments, check the schema page.

RSP setup: do this before the session¶

  1. Check that you have Rubin data rights. These include eligible US/Chilean scientists and students and named international data-rights holders.
  2. Open data.lsst.cloud, choose Log In, and authenticate through a supported identity provider (for example your institution, GitHub, or ORCID).
  3. Complete onboarding, verify your email, choose a username, and wait for account/data-rights approval. Start this before the workshop.
  4. After approval, return and open Notebooks.
  5. Upload this .ipynb using the JupyterLab file browser. Select the LSST kernel, then run cells in order using Shift–Enter.

When you launch a notebook on RSP, Rubin provides the required software and configures access using your logged-in account. You can usually connect to the catalog service (TAP) and image service (Butler) without entering a separate access token.

However, successfully importing a package only shows that the software is installed. To check that you can actually access DP2 data, Part 1 retrieves catalog rows and Part 2 retrieves an image cutout.

Account steps: official account guide. Environment help: RSP Notebook guide. Do not install a replacement LSST stack into the managed kernel for this lesson.

Optional: where NERSC and your DP1 reference differ¶

NERSC is a separate HPC platform: it needs its own account/project access and software setup. An RSP account does not create a NERSC account or guarantee a local Rubin repository there. Use NERSC Jupyter and your collaboration's current instructions. Modules, kernels, filesystem paths, credentials, and pipeline versions may differ.

In my DP1/NERSC, some relevant examples are repo_config="/global/cfs/cdirs/lsst/production/gen3/rubin/DP1/repo/butler.yaml" collection="LSSTComCam/DP1" instrument = 'LSSTComCam' skymap = 'lsst_cells_v1' butler = Butler(repo_config, collections="LSSTComCam/DP1"), and legacy geom.BoxI/MultibandExposure and the get_tap commands may be not available . Here the RSP DP2 route uses RSPDiscovery("dp2"), the dp2 collection, and lsst.images.Box/CellCoadd. These differences combine release/API changes with environment setup; they are not all consequences of NERSC itself.

All subsequent exercises assume RSP. Additional historical examples appear in the final cell.

Part 1 — Query and understand the Object catalog¶

1.1 Understand the columns first with the schema:¶

TAP exposes a database schema as tap_schema.columns. The schema browser is useful for reading descriptions. We will inspect a small set of columns rather than download the entire catalog.

The helper submits an asynchronous server job and waits for it in this notebook. If a query fails, its URL is retained for diagnosis. A TOP limit is a teaching safeguard, not a random sample; a result that reaches that limit may be incomplete.

In [3]:
def run_query(adql):
    job = tap.submit_job(adql)
    try:
        job.run()
        job.wait(phases=["COMPLETED", "ERROR", "ABORTED"], timeout=300)
        if job.phase == "ERROR":
            job.raise_if_error()
        if job.phase != "COMPLETED":
            raise RuntimeError(f"TAP job ended/waited in phase {job.phase}")
        result = job.fetch_result().to_table()
    except Exception:
        print("Inspect the TAP job:", job.url)
        raise
    else:
        job.delete()
        return result


schema = run_query("""
    SELECT column_name, datatype, unit, description
    FROM tap_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'dp2.Object'
""")
column_names = {str(name) for name in schema["column_name"]}
wanted = {"objectId", "coord_ra", "i_psfFlux", "i_cModelMag",
          "i_inputCount", "i_psfFlux_flag", "parentObjectId", "i_kronRad"}
schema[np.array([str(name) in wanted for name in schema["column_name"]])]

1.2 A small sky query¶

We use a 0.05-degree radius near ECDFS, not the entire named field. In ADQL, POINT defines each catalog position and CIRCLE defines our search region; CONTAINS(...)=1 retains positions inside it. Angles are in degrees here.

The example retrieves fluxes, magnitudes, morphology, and their relevant flags. Keep the first query broad so we can see the effect of subsequent cuts.

In [4]:
RA, DEC = 53.076, -28.110
RADIUS_DEG = 0.05
ROW_LIMIT = 5000
BAND = "i"

columns = ["objectId", "coord_ra", "coord_dec", "tract", "patch",
           "parentObjectId", "refBand", "refExtendedness",
           "detect_fromBlend", "detect_isIsolated"]
for b in ("g", "r", "i"):
    columns += [f"{b}_psfFlux", f"{b}_psfFluxErr", f"{b}_psfMag",
                f"{b}_cModelMag", f"{b}_cModel_flag", f"{b}_psfFlux_flag",
                f"{b}_inputCount", f"{b}_invalidPsfFlag",
                f"{b}_pixelFlags_saturatedCenter",
                f"{b}_pixelFlags_interpolatedCenter"]
missing = sorted(set(columns) - column_names)
if missing:
    raise RuntimeError(f"Expected DP2 columns missing; inspect the schema: {missing}")

cone = ("CONTAINS(POINT('ICRS', coord_ra, coord_dec), "
        f"CIRCLE('ICRS', {RA}, {DEC}, {RADIUS_DEG})) = 1")
query = f"SELECT TOP {ROW_LIMIT} {', '.join(columns)} FROM dp2.Object WHERE {cone}"
print(query)
objects = run_query(query)
print("Rows:", len(objects))
if not len(objects):
    raise ValueError("No objects returned. Check release, footprint, and search position.")
if len(objects) >= ROW_LIMIT:
    print("Row cap reached: reduce the radius before interpreting sample statistics.")
objects[:5]

1.3 Select usable measurements, then make a color¶

This demonstration uses g- and r-band CModel photometry for color and i-band PSF photometry for a signal-to-noise check. We require each matching failure flag to be false, inputs to exist, and the listed central-pixel/PSF checks to pass. We do not discard every blended object. The masks deliberately treat missing booleans as failures.

This is a local teaching selection; the same conditions can be pushed into an ADQL WHERE clause for a larger region. Classifying every extended object as a galaxy would need validation.

In [5]:
def numeric(column):
    return np.ma.asarray(column, dtype=float).filled(np.nan)


def is_false(column):
    # A masked value is unknown, so it must not pass a 'good flag' check.
    return ~np.ma.asarray(column, dtype=bool).filled(True)


# edit filters for flags here
def good_band(table, band, failure_flag):
    keep = numeric(table[f"{band}_inputCount"]) > 0
    for flag in (failure_flag, f"{band}_invalidPsfFlag",
                 f"{band}_pixelFlags_saturatedCenter",
                 f"{band}_pixelFlags_interpolatedCenter"):
        keep &= is_false(table[flag])
    return keep


flux = numeric(objects["i_psfFlux"])
flux_err = numeric(objects["i_psfFluxErr"])
snr = np.divide(flux, flux_err, out=np.full_like(flux, np.nan), where=flux_err > 0)
gmag, rmag = numeric(objects["g_cModelMag"]), numeric(objects["r_cModelMag"])
good_i = good_band(objects, "i", "i_psfFlux_flag") & np.isfinite(snr) & (snr > 5)
good_color = (good_band(objects, "g", "g_cModel_flag")
              & good_band(objects, "r", "r_cModel_flag")
              & np.isfinite(gmag) & np.isfinite(rmag))
selected = objects[good_i & good_color & (rmag > 18) & (rmag < 25)]
print(f"Returned: {len(objects)}; i-band checks/SNR: {good_i.sum()}; selected: {len(selected)}")
if not len(selected):
    print("Selection is empty: inspect which checks removed rows before loosening cuts.")

Returned: 2454; i-band checks/SNR: 1982; selected: 954

1.4 Keep IDs, units, and the query together¶

ECSV retains table metadata, units, masked values, and integer IDs more reliably than an unannotated CSV. We save into a relative dp2_intro_outputs directory under the notebook's working directory. Use your RSP home workspace for work you want to retain; scratch retention rules can differ.

In [7]:
import json
OUTPUT_DIR = Path("dp2_intro_outputs")
OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
selected.meta["release"] = RELEASE
selected.meta["rsp_image_tag"] = RSP_IMAGE_TAG
selected.meta["query"] = query
selected.meta["selection"] = "good g/r CModel + good i PSF; i SNR>5; 18<r<25"
selected.write(OUTPUT_DIR / "ecdfs_selected.ecsv", format="ascii.ecsv", overwrite=True)
(OUTPUT_DIR / "query_and_environment.json").write_text(json.dumps({
    "release": RELEASE, "rsp_image_tag": RSP_IMAGE_TAG,
    "query": query, "radius_deg": RADIUS_DEG, "row_limit": ROW_LIMIT,
    "selection": selected.meta["selection"], "python": sys.version,
}, indent=2))
print("Saved catalog and provenance under", OUTPUT_DIR.resolve())

Saved catalog and provenance under /home/xianghu/notebooks/tutorials/dp2_intro_outputs

Try it: change the radius to 0.01 degrees and rerun Part 1. How does the row count change? Then remove only the interpolation-center cut and compare the retained count. (Interpolation flag: It means that near this object’s center, at least one pixel used to build the coadd had its value estimated from nearby pixels, rather than using its original measured value.) Do not interpret a TOP-limited catalog as a representative field population.

Part 2 — Coadd cutouts, masks, and PSF models¶

2.1 Choose a point-like object for the PSF exercise¶

We first prefer an isolated, point-like object with usable i-band PSF photometry. The target comes from the actual query, so no private catalog is required. If none exists, the image/PSF exercise still works at a good object's position, but the later point-source residual exercise is skipped.

In [8]:
isolated = np.ma.asarray(objects["detect_isIsolated"], dtype=bool).filled(False)
point_like = numeric(objects["refExtendedness"]) == 0
star_indices = np.flatnonzero(good_i & isolated & point_like)
IS_STAR_CANDIDATE = bool(len(star_indices))
pool = star_indices if IS_STAR_CANDIDATE else np.flatnonzero(good_i)
if not len(pool):
    raise ValueError("No usable i-band target in this cone. Try another covered position.")
# Closest candidate to our field position, using ALL candidates.
coords = SkyCoord(numeric(objects["coord_ra"])[pool] * u.deg,
                  numeric(objects["coord_dec"])[pool] * u.deg)
separations = coords.separation(SkyCoord(RA * u.deg, DEC * u.deg))
target = objects[pool[int(np.argmin(separations.arcsec))]]
target_coord = SkyCoord(float(target["coord_ra"]) * u.deg,
                        float(target["coord_dec"]) * u.deg)
print("objectId:", int(target["objectId"]), "parentObjectId:", int(target["parentObjectId"]))
print("Point-like/isolated candidate:", IS_STAR_CANDIDATE)
print("Target (ICRS):", target_coord)

2.2 Find the coadd and read its coordinate information¶

Use a Butler spatial query, separate from the TAP query syntax. Overlapping patches can produce several references. Prefer the patch recorded in the Object row, and preserve its full dataId. Read just the sky_projection and bbox components before requesting pixels.

In [9]:
refs = list(butler.query_datasets(
    "deep_coadd",
    where="band.name = :band AND patch.region OVERLAPS POINT(:ra, :dec)",
    bind={"band": BAND, "ra": float(target["coord_ra"]), "dec": float(target["coord_dec"])},
))
if not refs:
    raise ValueError("No coadd in this band at the target. Check coverage and release availability.")
for candidate in refs:
    print(candidate.dataId)
matching = [r for r in refs if int(r.dataId["tract"]) == int(target["tract"])
            and int(r.dataId["patch"]) == int(target["patch"])]
ref = matching[0] if matching else refs[0]
data_id = ref.dataId
sky = butler.get("deep_coadd.sky_projection", dataId=data_id)
full_bbox = butler.get("deep_coadd.bbox", dataId=data_id)
xy = sky.sky_to_pixel(target_coord)
print("Selected dataId:", data_id)
print("Target in absolute tract pixels:", xy)

2.3 Retrieve a small cutout¶

Box.factory[y_start:y_stop, x_start:x_stop] uses exclusive stop bounds, like Python slices. The cutout keeps its absolute pixel origin. We clip the requested box to the patch and report clipping. The nominal coadd pixel scale is 0.2 arcsec, so a 30-arcsec side is approximately 150 pixels.

In [10]:
PIXEL_SCALE_ARCSEC = 0.2
SIDE_ARCSEC = 30.0
side_pixels = int(round(SIDE_ARCSEC / PIXEL_SCALE_ARCSEC))
x0 = int(round(xy.x)) - side_pixels // 2
y0 = int(round(xy.y)) - side_pixels // 2
requested_bbox = Box.factory[y0:y0 + side_pixels, x0:x0 + side_pixels]
bbox = full_bbox.intersection(requested_bbox)
if bbox.x.stop <= bbox.x.start or bbox.y.stop <= bbox.y.start:
    raise ValueError("Requested box does not intersect the selected image.")
if bbox != requested_bbox:
    print("Cutout clipped at patch boundary:", requested_bbox, "→", bbox)
cutout = butler.get(ref, parameters={"bbox": bbox})
print(type(cutout).__name__, cutout.bbox, cutout.image.array.shape)

CellCoadd [y=4347:4497, x=15196:15346] (150, 150)

2.4 Display pixels with the correct WCS¶

The FITS WCS generated for this bounding box uses the local array frame. origin='lower' places increasing y upward. The stretch is for visualization, not a change to data. The mask schema gives the actual condition names and bit layout for this image. In DP2, use mask.get(name) rather than assuming DP1 integer bit values.

In [11]:
def show_cutout(image, coordinate, title):
    wcs = image.sky_projection.as_fits_wcs(bbox=image.bbox)
    arr = image.image.array
    finite = arr[np.isfinite(arr)]
    if not finite.size:
        raise ValueError("No finite pixels to display.")
    lo, hi = ZScaleInterval().get_limits(finite)
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5))
    ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection=wcs)
    ax.imshow(arr, origin="lower", cmap="gray", vmin=lo, vmax=hi)
    tx, ty = wcs.world_to_pixel(coordinate)
    ax.plot(tx, ty, "o", mfc="none", mec="tab:orange", ms=14, label="Catalog position")
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="RA", ylabel="Dec")
    ax.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


show_cutout(cutout, target_coord, f"DP2 {BAND}-band deep_coadd: {int(target['objectId'])}")
print(cutout.mask.schema)

MaskSchema(<9 planes>, uint8)
In [12]:
mask_names = set(cutout.mask.schema.names)
bad_pixels = np.zeros(cutout.image.array.shape, dtype=bool)
for name in ("NO_DATA", "SATURATED", "COSMIC_RAY"):
    if name in mask_names:
        plane = cutout.mask.get(name)
        print(name, "fraction:", float(plane.mean()))
        bad_pixels |= plane
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
ax.imshow(bad_pixels, origin="lower", cmap="gray_r", vmin=0, vmax=1)
ax.set(title="NO_DATA or SATURATED — local array frame", xlabel="Local x", ylabel="Local y")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

NO_DATA fraction: 0.0
SATURATED fraction: 0.0
COSMIC_RAY fraction: 0.002577777777777778

DETECTED is informational, so do not reject every nonzero mask pixel. INTERPOLATED, COSMIC_RAY, and INEXACT_PSF require science-dependent interpretation. The last condition can be common in coadds; a blanket rejection may discard much of the image. Source: DP2 pixel mask planes.

2.5 Evaluate the local PSF¶

A kernel image is centered around the origin for convolution. A stellar image is centered at the target position in absolute pixels and includes the appropriate subpixel placement. Use the stellar image for the observed-stamp comparison below. The PSF is a model, not a cutout of a star.

Source: DP2 tutorial 205.1, section 2.

In [14]:
psf = butler.get("deep_coadd.psf", dataId=data_id)
kernel = psf.compute_kernel_image(x=xy.x, y=xy.y)
stellar = psf.compute_stellar_image(x=xy.x, y=xy.y)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4))
for ax, image, title in zip(axes, (kernel, stellar), ("PSF kernel", "PSF at target position")):
    ax.imshow(image.array, origin="lower", cmap="magma")
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Stamp x", ylabel="Stamp y")
    print(title, image.bbox, "sum:", float(np.sum(image.array)))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

PSF kernel [y=-17:18, x=-17:18] sum: 1.000002594367907
PSF at target position [y=4405:4440, x=15254:15289] sum: 0.9999930745763315

2.6 Compare the observed star with the PSF: no fitting¶

This follows the normalized-stamp comparison in DP2 tutorial 205.1, section 7. Retrieve observed pixels with exactly the stellar model's bounding box, divide each image by its own summed flux, and display their difference. No amplitude, background, or centroid is fitted. The previous two-coefficient fit was an addition to this synthesis and has been removed.

The official example uses stars selected by the PSF-calibration flag. Here we reuse the isolated point-like candidate from section 2.1; it need not be a PSF-calibration star. Background, neighboring light, and centroid errors can affect this simple comparison, so it is not a photometric estimator.

In [15]:
if not IS_STAR_CANDIDATE:
    print("No isolated point-like candidate: star comparison skipped.")
elif stellar.bbox.intersection(full_bbox) != stellar.bbox:
    print("PSF stamp crosses the patch boundary: comparison skipped.")
else:
    star_stamp = butler.get(ref, parameters={"bbox": stellar.bbox})
    observed = np.asarray(star_stamp.image.array, dtype=float).copy()
    template = np.asarray(stellar.array, dtype=float).copy()
    invalid = ~np.isfinite(observed) | ~np.isfinite(template)
    for name in ("NO_DATA", "SATURATED"):
        if name in set(star_stamp.mask.schema.names):
            invalid |= star_stamp.mask.get(name)
    if invalid.any():
        print("Invalid or saturated pixels in the stamp: choose another star.")
    elif observed.sum() <= 0 or template.sum() <= 0:
        print("Nonpositive summed flux: normalization skipped.")
    else:
        observed /= observed.sum()
        template /= template.sum()
        residual = observed - template
        vmax = max(float(np.max(np.abs(observed))), float(np.max(np.abs(template))))
        rmax = max(float(np.max(np.abs(residual))), np.finfo(float).eps)
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4))
        for ax, arr, title, limit in zip(
            axes, (observed, template, residual),
            ("Observed star (normalized)", "Local PSF (normalized)", "Observed − PSF"),
            (vmax, vmax, rmax),
        ):
            im = ax.imshow(arr, origin="lower", cmap="viridis", vmin=-limit, vmax=limit)
            ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Local x", ylabel="Local y")
            fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.7, label="Fraction of stamp flux")
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

2.7 A color-combined deep-coadd image¶

Use the same object as the executed DP2 Footprint and Deep Cutout Browser: objectId=755370947912953965, found near the input ICRS position RA=53.1246023°, Dec=−27.7404715°. The catalog centroid is approximately (53.124503°, −27.740241°); we retrieve its full precision from TAP. Both this RGB display and the Scarlet example below use this object. The earlier PSF exercise retains its independently selected star.

Match the reference's display settings: z → red, r → green, g → blue, field of view 100 / 1.5 arcsec, common division by 3631, and Lupton stretch=0.01. These are visualization settings, not a conversion to magnitudes. Read the same absolute pixel box in the same tract/patch for all bands so the channels align. Black pixels have missing or nonfinite data in at least one band.

In [ ]:
from astropy.visualization import make_lupton_rgb

BROWSER_OBJECT_ID = 755370947912953965  # exact ID printed by the reference notebook
BROWSER_RA, BROWSER_DEC = 53.1246023, -27.7404715  # reference input position, ICRS degrees
browser_objects = run_query(f"""
SELECT objectId, coord_ra, coord_dec, tract, patch, parentObjectId
FROM dp2.Object
WHERE objectId = {BROWSER_OBJECT_ID}
AND CONTAINS(POINT('ICRS', coord_ra, coord_dec),
             CIRCLE('ICRS', {BROWSER_RA}, {BROWSER_DEC}, {2.0 / 3600.0})) = 1
""")
if len(browser_objects) != 1:
    raise ValueError("The exact reference Object ID was not found at its reference location.")
browser_target = browser_objects[0]
browser_coord = SkyCoord(float(browser_target["coord_ra"]) * u.deg,
                         float(browser_target["coord_dec"]) * u.deg)
print("RGB and Scarlet objectId:", int(browser_target["objectId"]), "position:", browser_coord)
browser_refs = list(butler.query_datasets(
    "deep_coadd",
    where="band.name = :band AND patch.region OVERLAPS POINT(:ra, :dec)",
    bind={"band": "i", "ra": float(browser_target["coord_ra"]),
          "dec": float(browser_target["coord_dec"])},
))
browser_matching = [r for r in browser_refs
                    if int(r.dataId["tract"]) == int(browser_target["tract"])
                    and int(r.dataId["patch"]) == int(browser_target["patch"])]
if not browser_matching:
    raise ValueError("No i-band coadd in the exact reference object's catalog tract/patch.")
browser_data_id = browser_matching[0].dataId
browser_patch_data_id = {key: browser_data_id[key] for key in ("skymap", "tract", "patch")}
browser_sky = butler.get("deep_coadd.sky_projection", dataId=browser_data_id)
browser_bounds = butler.get("deep_coadd.bbox", dataId=browser_data_id)
browser_xy = browser_sky.sky_to_pixel(browser_coord)
browser_half_px = int(round((100.0 / 1.5 / 2.0) / PIXEL_SCALE_ARCSEC))
# Reproduce the reference's one-pixel center box padded on all sides.
browser_requested = Box.factory[
    round(browser_xy.y):round(browser_xy.y) + 1,
    round(browser_xy.x):round(browser_xy.x) + 1,
].padded(browser_half_px)
browser_bbox = browser_bounds.intersection(browser_requested)
if browser_bbox != browser_requested:
    print("RGB field clipped at patch edge:", browser_bbox)

def coadd_for_band(band, box):
    """Read an aligned subset in the reference object's tract and patch."""
    band_id = {**browser_patch_data_id, "band": band}
    bounds = butler.get("deep_coadd.bbox", dataId=band_id)
    if bounds.intersection(box) != box:
        raise ValueError(f"The requested box is not fully covered in {band}.")
    return butler.get("deep_coadd", dataId=band_id, parameters={"bbox": box})
In [27]:
rgb_bands = ("z", "r", "g")  # reference: red, green, blue display channels
rgb_cutouts = {band: coadd_for_band(band, browser_bbox) for band in rgb_bands}
arrays = [np.asarray(rgb_cutouts[b].image.array, dtype=float).copy() for b in rgb_bands]
valid_rgb = np.ones(arrays[0].shape, dtype=bool)
for band, arr in zip(rgb_bands, arrays):
    valid_rgb &= np.isfinite(arr)
    image = rgb_cutouts[band]
    if "NO_DATA" in set(image.mask.schema.names):
        valid_rgb &= ~image.mask.get("NO_DATA")
for arr in arrays:
    arr[~valid_rgb] = 0.0
RGB_WEIGHTS = (1.1, 1.1, 1.1)  # same order as rgb_bands: z, r, g
weights = np.asarray(RGB_WEIGHTS, dtype=float)
if weights.shape != (3,) or not np.all(np.isfinite(weights)) or np.any(weights < 0):
    raise ValueError("RGB_WEIGHTS must contain three finite nonnegative values.")
rgb = make_lupton_rgb(
    *(weight * arr / 3631.0 for weight, arr in zip(weights, arrays)),
    stretch=0.01,
)
rgb[~valid_rgb] = 0
wcs_rgb = rgb_cutouts["z"].sky_projection.as_fits_wcs(bbox=browser_bbox)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection=wcs_rgb)
ax.imshow(rgb, origin="lower")
tx, ty = wcs_rgb.world_to_pixel(browser_coord)
# ax.plot(tx, ty, "o", mfc="none", mec="white", ms=14)
ax.set(title=f"Reference object {BROWSER_OBJECT_ID}: z/r/g RGB", xlabel="RA", ylabel="Dec")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

2.8 Retrieve the reference object's persisted Scarlet model¶

Use browser_target from section 2.4a: objectId=755370947912953965, the exact source in the executed DP2 browser. Its saved reference output reports parent blend 755370947912944139. Retrieve its current parent ID from the catalog and verify it; do not substitute a different blended source.

Object Scarlet models are read through Butler with the reference object's skymap, tract, and patch, without band. This reads existing pipeline models; it does not fit Scarlet again. Run section 2.4a before these optional Scarlet cells.

In [22]:
RUN_SCARLET_INSPECTION = True
model_data = None
scarlet_target = None
stored_blend = None
if RUN_SCARLET_INSPECTION:
    scarlet_target = browser_target  # exact same object as the RGB example
    model_data_id = dict(browser_patch_data_id)
    model_data = butler.get("object_scarlet_models", dataId=model_data_id)
    print("Archive type:", type(model_data).__name__)
    scarlet_parent_id = int(scarlet_target["parentObjectId"])
    stored_blend = model_data.blends[scarlet_parent_id]
    if scarlet_parent_id not in model_data.blends:
        raise ValueError("The reference object's parent blend is absent from this archive.")
    stored_blend = model_data.blends[scarlet_parent_id]
    print("Scarlet source:", int(scarlet_target["objectId"]), "parent:", scarlet_parent_id)
    print("Stored blend type:", type(stored_blend).__name__)
else:
    print("Optional Scarlet archive inspection skipped.")

2.9 Display the source model and its deblend extent (optional)¶

Adapted from section 8 of the DP2 cutout browser. Traverse a hierarchical archive to find the leaf containing the reference child 755370947912953965, convert aligned CellCoadd subsets with .to_legacy(), and assemble the multiband observation required by the Scarlet display utilities. show_scene shows the intrinsic model, its rendered appearance, the observed blend, and residuals.

Labels identify the children; boxes mark each child's model bounding box. They help show the deblend/footprint extent, but are not the exact irregular detection footprint or a boundary within which every pixel belongs exclusively to one child. The display includes the whole blend because its sources overlap. Model bands and PSF attributes can differ across pipeline versions; the helper checks the spellings used in the reference and reports a clear error if absent.

In [29]:
if stored_blend is None:
    print("No selected Scarlet blend: optional model display skipped.")
else:
    from lsst.afw.image import MultibandExposure
    import lsst.meas.extensions.scarlet as mes
    import lsst.scarlet.lite as sl

    def archive_value(archive, names):
        for name in names:
            value = getattr(archive, name, None)
            if value is not None:
                return value
        metadata = getattr(archive, "metadata", None)
        if metadata is not None:
            for name in names:
                if name in metadata:
                    return metadata[name]
        raise AttributeError(f"Scarlet archive has no {names}; check the RSP pipeline version.")

    def flat_leaf_blends(node, label=""):
        children = getattr(node, 'children', None)
        if children:
            leaves = []
            for child_id, child in children.items():
                child_label = f"{label}.{child_id}" if label else str(child_id)
                leaves += flat_leaf_blends(child, label=child_label)
            return leaves
        return [(label or str(scarlet_parent_id), node)]

    leaves = flat_leaf_blends(stored_blend)
    model_psf = archive_value(model_data, ("model_psf", "psf"))
    observed_bands = tuple(archive_value(model_data, ("bands",)))
    print("Reference Object ID:", int(scarlet_target["objectId"]),
          "| catalog parent:", scarlet_parent_id, "| leaf blends:", len(leaves))
    norm = sl.display.AsinhMapping(minimum=0, stretch=10, Q=10)
    for leaf_label, leaf in leaves:
        print(f"Leaf {leaf_label}: {len(leaf.sources)} source(s), bbox={leaf.bbox}")
        y0, x0 = leaf.bbox.origin
        ny, nx = leaf.bbox.shape
        scene_bbox = Box.factory[y0:y0 + ny, x0:x0 + nx]
        legacy_bbox = mes.utils.scarletBoxToBBox(leaf.bbox)
        # Require the same whole scene box in every band.
        exposures = [coadd_for_band(b, scene_bbox).copy().to_legacy()
                     for b in observed_bands]
        multiband = MultibandExposure.fromExposures(observed_bands, exposures)
        observation = mes.utils.buildObservation(
            modelPsf=model_psf, psfCenter=legacy_bbox.getCenter(), mExposure=multiband,
        )
        blend = leaf.to_blend(observation)
        print(f"Leaf {leaf_label}: {len(blend.sources)} reconstructed children")
        sl.display.show_scene(
            blend, norm=norm, show_model=True, show_rendered=True,
            show_observed=True, show_residual=True, linear=False,
            add_boxes=False, add_labels=True, figsize=(12, 7),
        )
        plt.show()

Leaf 755370947912944139: 20 source(s), bbox=Box(shape=(229, 108), origin=(10976, 14345))

Try it: evaluate the PSF at a second point inside the same patch and compare its image. Why should an extended galaxy leave structure after subtraction of a point-source model? What would you check if a catalog object has no coadd in the requested band?

Troubleshooting and references¶

Symptom First check
No module named lsst... Select the RSP LSST kernel and a DP2-compatible image.
Authentication/authorization failure Account approval, data rights, active RSP session, and the service used.
Missing column / different image method Inspect the live schema and record the pipeline image tag. DP1 names need not transfer.
Empty catalog / no dataset reference Position, search radius, band coverage, and Early/full DP2 availability.
Cutout appears shifted Absolute tract pixels versus local array indices; construct WCS using the cutout bbox.
Poor PSF residuals Neighbors, saturation, centroid, background, morphology, and PSF validity.

For help, use the Rubin Community Support category. The DP2 field-selection and cutout notebooks informed the exercise flow; the DP1 footprintviewer is used only for the setup comparison and appendix. The two survey figures are embedded in the notebook so they remain visible after upload. For scientific use, follow the DP2 citation guidance and cite the DP2 dataset.

Appendix — optional DP1/NERSC reference (last cell)¶

These short examples come from my personal experiences. They are historical illustrations, not setup commands to execute in the RSP DP2 lesson.

1. Release and service selection

# The DP1/NERSC reference:
repo_config="/global/cfs/cdirs/lsst/production/gen3/rubin/DP1/repo/butler.yaml"
collection="LSSTComCam/DP1"
instrument = 'LSSTComCam'
skymap = 'lsst_cells_v1'
butler = Butler(repo_config, collections="LSSTComCam/DP1")
# SQL in that notebook uses FROM dp1.Object.

# This notebook's RSP/DP2 equivalent:
discovery = RSPDiscovery("dp2")
tap = discovery.get_tap_client()
butler = Butler("dp2", collections=["dp2"])
# SQL here uses FROM dp2.Object.

Repository aliases and credentials are configured by the environment. A NERSC kernel may need a local repository configuration and collaboration-provided pipeline setup; there is no universal path to substitute. Butler access for DP2 repo at NERSC: (A confluence account required).

2. Cutout and image interfaces

# The reference constructs a legacy lsst.geom.BoxI and uses Exposure APIs.
# This DP2 lesson constructs an lsst.images.Box:
bbox = Box.factory[y0:y1, x0:x1]  # y first; stop bounds are exclusive
cutout = butler.get(ref, parameters={"bbox": bbox})  # CellCoadd
wcs = cutout.sky_projection.as_fits_wcs(bbox=cutout.bbox)
psf_image = cutout.psf.compute_stellar_image(x=xy.x, y=xy.y)

3. Scarlet reconstruction needs a version-aware bridge

DP1 uses modelData.psf, blend_data.bands, MultibandExposure.fromButler(..., "deep_coadd", ...), and a monkey-patched minimal_data_to_blend helper. Do not copy those assumptions into DP2. The supplied DP2 browser instead inspects hierarchical blend leaves and converts each coadd subset with .to_legacy() before assembling MultibandExposure.fromExposures(...) for legacy Scarlet utilities. PSF/band attributes and the stored hierarchy still need checking against the selected pipeline version. Section 2.8 now adapts that bridge to display one existing blend; it does not rerun the deblender.

In [ ]:
